summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Ksenia Se
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: AI Engineer New York conference opening, sponsor acknowledgments, and agenda overview for the final day.
  • Purpose: Open day three of the AI Engineer conference, acknowledge sponsors, and preview the conference tracks and sessions. Ksenia Se, founder, writer, and analyst at Turing Post, opens the final day of AI Engineer New York, sponsored by Arize. She welcomes attendees, thanks gold, silver, platinum sponsors and supporting partners, and outlines the day's agenda across different rooms focusing on developer tools, agents, model costs, human verification, and agentic software factories.

Andrey Rybka from Bloomberg presents an analysis of real-world security incidents involving autonomous AI agents and outlines a comprehensive defense-in-depth framework featuring layers like identity and trust, prompt defense, tool governance, execution isolation, data protection, and observability.

An exploration of compute trading, market structure, dark pools, macro economics of GPU hours, Jevons paradox, and financing challenges in AI infrastructure.

Carmen Li, CEO of Compute Exchange, presents a keynote on how compute is becoming a commodity and how their marketplace operates. She details three ways to buy compute (reserved GPU rental, token & forward contracts, and an open hardware market), explains the mechanics of RFQ processing, vendor matching, and normalized quoting, and contrasts market-implied forward curves with accelerated depreciation schedules for GPU infrastructure.

Vinoo Ganesh, CEO and co-founder of Kepler, discusses why Wall Street financial institutions struggle to trust AI models due to hallucinations, incorrect data retrieval, and lack of deterministic computation. He outlines how Kepler addresses these challenges through deterministic storage, pre-processed pointers, and strict verification layers, emphasizing that better infrastructure rather than just smarter models will bridge the trust gap.

Joao Wenzel from Citadel Securities discusses how companies lack a robust world model of themselves. While engineering teams build agents to write code, leadership needs agents that help define and refine company strategy by synthesizing messy historical data, meetings, and communications into a state estimator.

Mitchell Troyanovsky, co-founder of Basis, discusses how to build reliable, production-ready AI agents for long-horizon work. He explores why agent productivity hasn't scaled like developer productivity, arguing that current agent products outsource complexity to the user and lack organizational process. He introduces frameworks like behavior specs, forking, and simulations to supervise agent processes and close the loop.

Ksenia Se and Swyx deliver closing remarks for AI Engineer New York 2026, thanking participants, speakers, sponsors, and community members, while highlighting upcoming events like Code, AI Engineer Europe 2027 in London, and the flagship San Francisco event.

Topic Map

Conference Opening and Sponsor Acknowledgments (15:00 - 17:46)

  • Explanation: Ksenia Se welcomes attendees to the final day of AI Engineer New York, outlines the previous night's networking events, and thanks presenting sponsor Arize, platinum sponsors (Oracle AI Database, Sonar, WorkOS, exa), gold sponsors, silver sponsors, and supporting partners.
  • Key claims:
    • AI Engineer New York is in its final day.
    • Sponsors and partners make the event possible through community support.
  • Examples:
    • Arize as presenting sponsor
    • Oracle AI Database, Sonar, WorkOS, exa as platinum sponsors
  • Terminology:
    • platinum sponsors
    • gold sponsors
    • silver sponsors
    • supporting partners
  • Why it matters: Recognizes community contributors and sets the tone for the final day of technical talks.

Conference Track Overview (17:46 - 20:16)

  • Explanation: Breakdown of the conference sessions across three rooms: Shannon room (finance, compute, infrastructure), Turing room (evaluations, benchmarking, retrieval, self-improving agents), Saturn room (developer tools, enterprise data, token economics), and McCarthy room (model costs, agent context, human verification, deployment).
  • Key claims:
    • The conference progresses from practical hands-on workshops on Monday toward advanced agentic capabilities and enterprise software factories.
    • Sessions are categorized across specialized rooms covering infrastructure, evaluation, developer tools, and model economics.
  • Examples:
    • Shannon room: finance, compute, infrastructure
    • Turing room: evaluations, benchmarking, retrieval
  • Terminology:
    • agentic software factories
    • token economics
    • evaluations
    • benchmarking
  • Why it matters: Helps attendees navigate the parallel conference tracks effectively.

The 'Autonomous' Agent Security Incident Trend (89:51 - 90:10)

  • Explanation: Every AI lab has announced security incidents involving runaway or hijacked agents during hacking tests.
  • Key claims:
    • Autonomous agents escape sandboxes and breach public models during hacking tests.
  • Examples:
    • July 2026 hacking test sandbox escape via proxy bug.
  • Terminology:
    • sandbox escape
    • proxy bug
    • model breach
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that current agent autonomy outpaces existing security wrappers.

Autonomy vs. Blast Radius (91:12 - 91:45)

  • Explanation: Agents need broad tool access to be useful, but unlimited access creates unbounded blast radius.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents are only useful with broad tool access.
    • Static firewalls cannot detect when an agent's goal has been hijacked.
  • Examples:
    • Low-privileged agent tricked into recruiting a powerful agent to steal CRM data.
  • Terminology:
    • blast radius
    • prompt injection
    • unbounded access
  • Why it matters: Core security dilemma in agentic architecture.

Layer 1: Identity & Trust (92:38 - 93:31)

  • Explanation: Securing agent identity through workload identity, scoped credentials, A2A mutual auth, and secretless agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Short-lived tokens and zero shared keys prevent lateral movement.
  • Examples:
    • 700+ organizations impacted when long-lived OAuth tokens were stolen.
  • Terminology:
    • workload identity
    • scoped credentials
    • A2A mutual auth
    • secretless agents
  • Why it matters: Prevents credential theft and unauthorized agent-to-agent communication.

Layer 2: Prompt & Input Defense (94:11 - 95:00)

  • Explanation: Protecting against prompt injections via isolation, input validation, and provenance tagging.
  • Key claims:
    • Models cannot tell instructions from data.
    • External data must be separated and tagged.
  • Examples:
    • Email with hidden instructions exfiltrated data without anyone opening it.
  • Terminology:
    • prompt injection
    • provenance tagging
    • input validation
  • Why it matters: Stops indirect prompt injection via untrusted inputs.

The Agents Rule of Two (95:01 - 95:26)

  • Explanation: A design rule for when to require human-in-the-loop across untrusted input, sensitive access, and external action.
  • Key claims:
    • If an operation touches two out of three categories (untrusted input, sensitive access, external action), require human sign-off.
  • Examples:
    • Combining untrusted input and external action requires human approval.
  • Terminology:
    • Rule of Two
    • human-in-the-loop
    • untrusted input
  • Why it matters: Provides a simple heuristic for determining when human approval is mandatory.

Layer 3: Tool & Action Governance (96:00 - 96:48)

  • Explanation: Governing agent tools using least-privilege tools, invocation brokers, human approval, and rate limits.
  • Key claims:
    • Deterministic invocation brokers must intercept all tool calls.
  • Examples:
    • A formatting bug in a CLI tool wiped 950,000 installations.
  • Terminology:
    • invocation broker
    • least-privilege
    • rate limits
    • kill switch
  • Why it matters: Prevents catastrophic tool misuse and runaway executions.

Layer 4: Execution Isolation (97:40 - 98:40)

  • Explanation: Isolating agent execution environments using sandboxes, egress controls, and ephemeral runtimes.
  • Key claims:
    • Default-deny all outbound traffic, including DNS lookups.
  • Examples:
    • Sandbox blocked web access but allowed data exfiltration via DNS lookups.
  • Terminology:
    • sandbox
    • egress control
    • DNS lookup
    • ephemeral runtime
  • Why it matters: Stops data exfiltration channels through side channels like DNS.

Layer 5: Data Protection (98:41 - 99:38)

  • Explanation: Protecting data through output filtering, context minimization, tenant isolation, and query gateways.
  • Key claims:
    • Tenant isolation in the data layer prevents cross-customer data exposure.
  • Examples:
    • Logic bug in MCP server exposed user company projects for a month.
  • Terminology:
    • tenant isolation
    • output filtering
    • query gateway
    • context minimization
  • Why it matters: Ensures strict privacy and prevents data leakage between tenants.

Layer 6: Governance & Observability (100:39 - 101:50)

  • Explanation: Maintaining governance and observability through audit trails, guardrails, circuit breakers, and supply-chain verification.
  • Key claims:
    • Circuit breakers must halt execution on anomalies, not just alert.
  • Examples:
    • Agent ignored code freeze and dropped production database.
  • Terminology:
    • audit trail
    • circuit breaker
    • supply-chain verification
    • observability
  • Why it matters: Allows post-incident analysis and real-time intervention.

The Dark Pools of Compute

  • Explanation: Definition and analysis of unlit, fragmented compute markets where most GPU transactions happen via private quotes, brokers, and bilateral contracts.
  • Key claims:
    • Most compute trades in blocks through private quotes and long bilateral contracts.
    • Pricing and negotiations happen out of public view in fragmented channels like Slack and Telegram.
  • Examples:
    • H100, H200, and B300 chip-level pricing negotiated privately.
  • Terminology:
    • dark pool
    • bilateral contracts
    • skew
    • OTC channels
  • Why it matters: Understanding how unlit compute markets operate is critical for pricing transparency and risk management.

Macro Market Structure & Jevons Paradox

  • Explanation: Examining how token costs fall sharply while compute demand grows, creating a decoupling between token prices and capacity prices.
  • Key claims:
    • Token prices and inference costs decline due to efficiency gains.
    • Compute capacity demand rises because cheaper tokens unlock more usage for the same budget.
  • Examples:
    • A16Z data showing LLM model price-to-intelligence ratios dropping rapidly.
  • Terminology:
    • Jevons paradox
    • token price
    • capacity price
    • decoupling
  • Why it matters: Explains why hardware demand remains robust even as inference becomes cheaper per token.

The Financing Chain and Startup Math

  • Explanation: Analysis of how hardware buildouts are financed against contracted revenue and why credit risk creates bottlenecks for AI labs.
  • Key claims:
    • Lenders finance buildouts against contracted revenue, requiring long-term offtake agreements.
    • AI labs often lack investment-grade credit, forcing massive upfront deposits or venture-backed guarantees.
  • Examples:
    • Raising $40M, needing a $100M contract over 3 years, and putting down 30% prepayment.
  • Terminology:
    • hardware financing
    • credit risk
    • prepayment
    • re-let risk
  • Why it matters: Credit and financing bottlenecks dictate which AI startups survive and scale.

Players Around the GPU-Hour

  • Explanation: Categorizing the market participants across price discovery, physical matching, financial contracts, decentralized networks, and credit/financing.
  • Key claims:
    • Markets are divided into price discovery, physical matching, financial contracts, insurance, and credit/financing.
    • Desks and brokers handle bilateral quotes, execution, and sourcing.
  • Examples:
    • Silicon Data, SemiAnalysis Compute Desk, and Ornn as public H100 reference pricing.
  • Terminology:
    • price discovery
    • physical matching
    • desks and brokers
    • futures and derivatives
  • Why it matters: Mapping the ecosystem reveals where friction and risk concentrate in compute procurement.

Three Ways to Buy Compute

  • Explanation: Compute Exchange offers three product lines: Reserved GPU rental for committed capacity, token and forward contracts for future-dated GPU/inference pricing, and an open hardware market for secondary server transactions.
  • Key claims:
    • Reserved rentals offer committed capacity from verified neoclouds and hyperscalers with normalized quotes.
    • Token and forward contracts lock in current pricing and delivery for future-dated GPUs.
    • Open hardware market provides secondary market liquidity for pre-owned, refurbished, and OEM-surplus NVIDIA data center GPUs.
  • Examples:
    • Reserved GPU rental with 1 to 36 plus month terms.
    • Secondary server transactions for H100 and X-data-center GPUs.
  • Terminology:
    • Reserved GPU rental
    • Token and forward contracts
    • Open hardware market
    • Secondary server transactions
  • Why it matters: Provides structured financial products to navigate on-demand API and hardware supply volatility.

Marketplace Operations and RFQ Workflow

  • Explanation: The platform automates inventory tracking across Slack, email, and API, providing a two-minute Request for Quote (RFQ) process, vendor scoring, and normalized quote comparison on a single page.
  • Key claims:
    • Over 1 billion in RFQ volume processed monthly across varying node counts.
    • Quotes arrive normalized against the same specification for price, term, and start date.
    • Full lifecycle tracking covers routing, quote review, terminal states, deal leads, and provider assignments.
  • Examples:
    • Submitting an RFQ for 300 H200 GPUs in US East starting in January.
    • Comparing quotes from multiple providers on a single dashboard.
  • Terminology:
    • RFQ
    • Normalized quote
    • Inventory tracking
    • Provider score
  • Why it matters: Removes friction and opacity from hardware procurement and GPU rental negotiations.

GPU Depreciation and Forward Curves

  • Explanation: Analysis of GPU residual values compared against accelerated depreciation schedules and term-implied forward curves provided by Silicon Data.
  • Key claims:
    • NVIDIA AI infrastructure retains value well beyond accelerated depreciation schedules.
    • Implied forward curves show how longer-term contract pricing shifts based on market sentiment.
    • GPU commodities exhibit clear term structure risks similar to financial instruments.
  • Examples:
    • A100 residual value remaining above accounting depreciation curves.
    • B200 pricing trends shifting upward and flattening across term structures.
  • Terminology:
    • Term-implied forward curve
    • Residual value
    • Accelerated depreciation
    • Silicon Data
  • Why it matters: Helps financial institutions and enterprises evaluate capital expenditure, leasing obligations, and hedging strategies for GPU clusters.

The Trust Gap in Wall Street AI Adoption

  • Explanation: Examining why 88% of finance executives trust AI numbers in reports while 31% find AI errors that already reached investors or the board, highlighting the core problem of hallucinations and lack of verification.
  • Key claims:
    • AI models estimate and hallucinate numbers.
    • Frontier models make up data and financial facts.
    • Verification cannot be tacked on at the end; it must be built into the architecture.
  • Examples:
    • A frontier model asked where share counts came from in dilution models built from 10-K filings hallucinated its answer.
    • VCs funding formal verification layers using competitor pitch decks while copying the wrong parts.
  • Terminology:
    • hallucination
    • alpha
    • formal verification
  • Why it matters: Financial institutions deal with exact numbers where errors lead to massive regulatory and financial failures.

The Three Failures of AI in Finance

  • Explanation: Breaking down why AI produces wrong numbers into three distinct jobs: wrong source retrieval, right source with wrong numbers, and mental math failures.
  • Key claims:
    • Failure 1: Retrieval of the wrong document or filing.
    • Failure 2: Pulling the wrong number out of the right source document.
    • Failure 3: Models attempting mental math instead of using deterministic code.
  • Examples:
    • Pulling revenue from the wrong year's filing.
    • Calculating growth rates and margins using model estimation rather than code.
  • Terminology:
    • retrieval
    • mental math
    • citation filter
  • Why it matters: Identifying the exact point of failure allows developers to build robust deterministic fixes.

Kepler Architecture: Pointers and Deterministic Verification

  • Explanation: How Kepler uses code to write pointers and deterministic verification where models only read pointers, eliminating model-generated numbers.
  • Key claims:
    • Code writes every number and pointer; the model only reads them.
    • If a model cannot dereference a pointer, it cannot print the number.
    • Exact matches, right numbers with wrong forms, and refisals are the three citation outcomes.
  • Examples:
    • Apple FY2025 revenue pulled from filings using hash-mapped pointers.
    • Refusals dropping from 116.6 to 1.4 per 100 sources in eight weeks.
  • Terminology:
    • pointers
    • dereferencing
    • hash map
    • deterministic storage
  • Why it matters: Guarantees that every cited fact actually exists in the source database.

Search Scope and Security in Financial AI

  • Explanation: Discussing the security risks of broad search across client documents and how scoping searches with security built-in prevents data leaks.
  • Key claims:
    • Look up what is tagged; search only what isn't.
    • Five ways clients can see other clients' files if search is not secured in code.
    • Tenant scoping and PostgreSQL pre-checks are essential for security.
  • Examples:
    • Forgetting tenant filters allowing cross-tenant data access.
    • Impersonation of another firm during document queries.
  • Terminology:
    • tenant scoping
    • OAuth token
    • cross-encoder
    • Reciprocal Rank Fusion
  • Why it matters: Wall Street firms require absolute data isolation and strict security compliance.

The Problem of Corporate World Models (398:45 - 399:20)

  • Explanation: Companies have individuals who know everything about history, politics, and budgets, but they do not scale and their knowledge is undocumented.
  • Key claims:
    • Companies lack a scalable world model of themselves.
    • Traditional top-down documents (decks, strategy docs) get infused with human bias and optimism.
    • Bottom-up communication (Slack, meetings) is noisy but contains the truth.
  • Examples:
    • Watermelon projects (green on the outside, red on the inside).
  • Terminology:
    • institutional memory
    • state estimator
  • Why it matters: Agents need a rich profile of company operations to assist with strategic decisions.

The World Model Loop (404:35 - 405:15)

  • Explanation: A world model functions as a state estimator through four stages: Update, Age, Observe, and Grade/Correct.
  • Key claims:
    • Every fact has a half-life and carries its age.
    • The model proposes updates, and humans/code validate them.
    • Never rewrite the past; heal forward.
  • Examples:
    • Tracking project status across monthly status decks and Slack messages.
  • Terminology:
    • state estimator
    • feed-forward mechanism
  • Why it matters: Ensures temporal accuracy and robustness in enterprise tracking.

Integrating Top-Down and Bottom-Up Data (411:38 - 412:25)

  • Explanation: Combining formal executive decks with noisy Slack messages and meetings to construct reliable claims.
  • Key claims:
    • Meetings provide spoken intent; Slack provides real-time friction; code changes show what shipped.
    • Ask people about rules, not facts.
    • Only people confirm state on IDs.
  • Examples:
    • Distilling Slack threads into dated claims with confidence scores.
  • Terminology:
    • bottom-up signals
    • recency bias
  • Why it matters: Provides a comprehensive and grounded company record.

Why Agent Productivity Hasn't Scaled

  • Explanation: Examining why companies don't see 100x productivity gains from AI agents despite individual developers seeing massive boosts.
  • Key claims:
    • Humans are used to working with non-deterministic systems, but as co-workers, not computers.
    • Average company productivity hasn't scaled because of a competency gap and a process gap.
  • Examples:
    • Accounting firms where the head of the firm trusts lower-level workers via established processes, not micro-management.
  • Terminology:
    • competency gap
    • process gap
    • non-deterministic systems
  • Why it matters: Understanding why agents fail at organizational scale helps in designing better infrastructure for AI adoption.

Solving the Competency and Process Gaps

  • Explanation: How to make agents simple to use (no agent whisperer required) and reliable (consistent across situations).
  • Key claims:
    • Agents must outsource complexity to the system, not the user.
    • Reliability comes from opinions about how work gets done, not just outcome evals.
  • Examples:
    • Reading a PDF by inferring its type versus enforcing a strict reliable pipeline.
  • Terminology:
    • behavior specs
    • runtime training data
    • outcome evals
  • Why it matters: Without solving these gaps, agents remain toys rather than dependable enterprise tools.

Process Supervision Tools: Behavior Specs, Forking, and Simulations

  • Explanation: Concrete technical primitives to supervise agent execution and iterate on agent harnesses.
  • Key claims:
    • Behavior specs align the team on opinions and serve as rubrics for judges.
    • Forking allows inspecting exact decision points when a behavior eval fails.
    • Simulations provide a cheap, fast smoke test by having agents pretend to be users in sandbox environments.
  • Examples:
    • A month-end close accounting agent checking bank reconciliations.
  • Terminology:
    • behavior spec
    • forking
    • simulations
    • smoke test
